behavior_items: The source is a C++20/23 module interface unit with a global module fragment: `module;` places the following `#include <boost/json.hpp>` into the global module fragment so the Boost headers are textually included before the named module declaration rather than being attached to the module `repro` itself.

Including `boost/json.hpp` in the global module fragment causes the compiler to parse and instantiate a very large header-defined API surface before it sees `export module repro;`. This exercises GCC's modules implementation on a translation unit that contains extensive preprocessor state, many declarations, templates, namespaces, inline entities, and source locations originating from the included header graph.

The named module declaration `export module repro;` turns the file into a module interface unit and requires GCC to begin producing compiled module metadata for the interface. Because the unit is compiled with `-fmodules`, GCC must serialize exported entities, attachment information, and source-location data into the GCM/module representation.

The only user-declared exported API is `export namespace boost::json { using boost::json::visit; }`. This does not define a new function; it re-exports an existing declaration from the included Boost namespace into the module interface so importers of `repro` can see `boost::json::visit` as part of the module's exported surface.

That exported `using` declaration is significant because it forces GCC to treat a declaration originating from the global-module-fragment include as part of the module interface's exported API. This exercises the compiler path that maps declarations coming from a header included before the module declaration into exported module metadata, including their ownership and source-location provenance.

The reproducer therefore stresses the interaction between three features at once: global module fragment inclusion of a large header library, module-interface serialization, and export of an aliasing/using declaration that refers to preexisting header declarations rather than to a fresh declaration authored after `export module`.

The command line reinforces this path: `-std=c++2b -fmodules` enables the modules implementation; `-c` compiles only; `-x c++ -fpreprocessed -fdirectives-only` tells GCC it is consuming a preprocessed reproduction file while still honoring directives needed to preserve enough structural information for module handling. This means the crash is not dependent on normal preprocessing, but on later semantic/module-writing phases.

The failure point `internal compiler error: in write_location, at cp/module.cc:17560` indicates the compiler gets past parsing and into module emission/serialization. `write_location` strongly suggests GCC is attempting to encode a source location associated with some exported or reachable declaration and encounters an internal inconsistency instead of issuing a normal user-facing diagnostic.

Because the ICE is reported at the line `export module repro;`, the visible location is likely just where GCC begins or attributes the module-interface export work, not necessarily where the underlying malformed internal state was created. The real trigger is more plausibly some declaration from the included Boost headers that becomes reachable/exported through `using boost::json::visit;` and later causes location serialization to fail.

The bug report's note about a minimally modified Boost to avoid unrelated TU-exposure issues suggests the reproducer intentionally isolates this crash from other known modules/header problems. In other words, after sidestepping separate exposure diagnostics, the remaining behavior is a compiler correctness bug: GCC ICEs on valid or near-valid module-interface code instead of accepting it or producing a standard diagnostic.

Semantically, the program is trivial: it creates a module named `repro` whose exported surface consists of an existing Boost.JSON name. There is no algorithmic runtime behavior; the entire reproducer is about compile-time name visibility, namespace export, and module boundary formation.

The core compiler behavior exercised is GCC's need to reconcile declaration origin and attachment across the global module fragment and named module interface. A declaration defined in included headers must remain usable, be associated with the correct semantic context, and carry serializable location information when exposed through an exported `using` declaration. The ICE shows that this bookkeeping breaks in the tested GCC revision.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: The reproducer is a minimal module-interface test that includes `boost/json.hpp` in the global module fragment, declares `export module repro;`, and re-exports `boost::json::visit` via an exported `using` declaration. Its purpose is to force GCC's modules machinery to serialize an exported interface that references declarations originating from a large header included before the module declaration. GCC 15.0.1 parses far enough to start writing module metadata, then crashes in `cp/module.cc::write_location`, showing an internal failure in source-location/declaration serialization for this global-module-fragment plus exported-header-name scenario rather than a normal compile-time diagnostic.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The failure pattern points to GCC's C++ modules serialization layer, not parsing or Boost-specific semantics. Common traits are: (1) a global module fragment textually includes a very large header graph before the named module declaration; (2) the interface then exports only a `using` declaration that refers to an existing declaration from that pre-module header content; (3) compilation uses `-fmodules` on a preprocessed file, so preprocessing is largely removed and the crash happens in later module-writing code; and (4) the ICE occurs in `cp/module.cc:write_location`, which strongly indicates bad bookkeeping for a source location attached to a declaration being written into module metadata. The most likely compiler-side issue is that GCC mis-handles declarations originating in the global module fragment when they become reachable/exported through an aliasing `using` declaration in a named module interface. That can leave the serializer with an invalid, unmapped, synthetic, or otherwise non-serializable `location_t`, or with the wrong ownership/attachment metadata for the declaration, causing `write_location` to ICE when emitting the GCM.
possible_causes: Bug in `cp/module.cc` location serialization for declarations exported from a module interface but originating in the global module fragment, leading to an invalid or unsupported `location_t` reaching `write_location`.

Incorrect module ownership/attachment propagation for an exported `using` declaration that names an entity from header code included before `export module`, so GCC serializes the target declaration as if it belonged to the interface without properly normalizing its provenance.

Failure to handle alias/re-export metadata for namespace-scope `using` declarations in modules, especially when the referenced declaration is preexisting and header-defined rather than newly declared after the module declaration.

Missing guard or remapping logic for source locations coming from preprocessed/directives-only input during module emission, exposed when large included headers create macro-expanded or synthetic locations that later become part of exported module state.

Reachability/export graph bug in module writer: GCC may traverse and serialize too much of the referenced Boost declaration graph, eventually encountering a declaration/location form that module emission does not expect for GMF-originated entities.

Defect in merging header-unit/global-module-fragment declarations with named-module interface metadata, causing stale or uninitialized source-location/state fields on declarations re-exported through `using`.

The repro still crashes when using a preprocessed file with `-fpreprocessed -fdirectives-only`, which indicates the bug is stable in later semantic/module-writing phases and not dependent on ordinary preprocessing behavior.

gcc/cp/decl.cc.summary: We're initializing a local variable which has a cleanup GUARD. If there are any temporaries used in the initializer INIT of this variable, we need to wrap their cleanups with TRY_CATCH_EXPR (, GUARD) so that the variable will be cleaned up properly if one of them throws. Unfortunately, there's no way to express this properly in terms of nesting, as the regions for the temporaries overlap the region for the variable itself; if there are two temporaries, the variable needs to be the first thing destroyed if either of the temporary destructors throws. However, we only want to run the variable's cleanup if it actually got constructed. So we need to guard the temporary cleanups with the variable's cleanup if they are run on the normal path, but not if they are run on the exceptional path. We implement this by telling honor_protect_cleanup_actions to strip the variable cleanup from the exceptional path. Another approach could be to make the variable cleanup region enclose initialization, but depend on a flag to indicate that the variable is initialized; that's effectively what we do for arrays. But the current approach works fine for non-arrays, and has no code overhead in the usual case

gcc/c-family/c-lex.cc.summary: Convert a series of STRING, WSTRING, STRING16, STRING32 and/or UTF8STRING tokens into a tree, performing string constant concatenation. TOK is the first of these. VALP is the location to write the string into. OBJC_STRING indicates whether an '@' token preceded the incoming token (in that case, the strings can either be ObjC strings, preceded by a single '@', or normal strings, not preceded by '@'. The result will be a CPP_OBJC_STRING). Returns the CPP token type of the result (CPP_STRING, CPP_WSTRING, CPP_STRING32, CPP_STRING16, CPP_UTF8STRING, or CPP_OBJC_STRING). This is unfortunately more work than it should be. If any of the strings in the series has an L prefix, the result is a wide string (6.4.5p4). Whether or not the result is a wide string affects the meaning of octal and hexadecimal escapes (6.4.4.4p6,9). But escape sequences do not continue across the boundary between two strings in a series (6.4.5p7), so we must not lose the boundaries. Therefore cpp_interpret_string takes a vector of cpp_string structures, which we must arrange to provide.
Converts a (possibly wide) character constant token into a tree.
